newsitem.title: CANADA: British Columbia promises cuts, but no surplus.
newsitem.headline: British Columbia promises cuts, but no surplus.

text.p: British Columbia plans to save C$500 million a year by eliminating 3,500 civil service jobs as part of a major austerity plan, provincial Premier Glen Clark said on Tuesday evening.
However, in a television address, Clark steered clear of promising to deliver on a projected budget surplus.

He said that, as part of the cuts, his government would remove a large portion of B.C.'s current C$126 million in annual subsidies to business and reduce grants to municipalities that currently total C$400 million per year.
Another C$50 million is to be saved by lowering the province's administration of health care as well as C$17 million by steering civil legal disputes from the courts into mediation.
"I think it's important that everyone carries their share of the burden when cuts are being made," Clark said, stressing that B.C.'s government would take the biggest fiancial hits.
Clark's government has been under attack over its finances after accusations it deceived voters over the state of the budget.
The province said in July it had a C$235 million deficit in the fiscal year to March 31 rather than a C$16 million surplus as forecast in April.
Opposition politicians claim the government withheld that news until after a May provincial election in which the New Democratic Party held onto power by a slim margin.
In Tuesday's address, Clark did not promise to make good on a C$88-million surplus projected in his June budget for 1996/97. "There we have, so far, failed to deliver."

A poll released Tuesday by the Province newspaper and UTV television found that 75.4 percent of those polled believed the government knew about the deficit before the election and deliberately withheld the news from voters.
In the first fiscal quarter to June 30, the province recorded a budget deficit of C$463 million compared to a C$228 million deficit in the same period a year earlier.
In announcing the first quarter figures, the government said in September it planned to cut spending by C$750 million over 18 months. It has also frozen capital spending.

Although the province has not officially revised its surplus projection, officials have said it may be a challenge to achieve a balanced budget this year, citing weaker than expected economic growth and a shortfall in revenues.

Private economists and opposition politicians have said that the government relied on only the most optimistic growth forecasts in drafting the budget despite warnings of a likely softening in the economy this year.
